concept.name: Rounding top
concept.definition: A long-term bearish reversal pattern, the mirror of the rounding bottom, in which an advance gradually flattens into an inverted-U or dome shape and then curves downward as sentiment shifts slowly from bullish to bearish. It is interpreted as a distribution process — informed holders selling gradually without disturbing the price — and is confirmed when price breaks down from the dome's base. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law.
concept.intuition: Buyers lose the power to push price higher but sellers exit slowly, so the chart rolls over in a gentle dome rather than a spike; once the artificial support of patient distribution ends, price falls away.
concept.mechanics: Price rounds over after an extended uptrend, with volume typically highest at both ends of the pattern and lowest in the middle (an inverted volume saucer). The pattern is confirmed when price falls from the edge of the dome, often with a volume pickup; rounding tops usually take less time to form than rounding bottoms. There is no standard measured target; some analysts project the depth of the inverted U.
concept.failure_modes: Gradual domes frequently resolve upward — a renewed breakout through the dome's high turns the 'distribution' into a continuation base, so acting before the downside break is the main error. The pattern's rarity and long formation time make clean examples scarce.
concept.misconceptions: That a rounding top needs a sharp breakdown to be valid — the defining feature is the gradual rollover; confirmation is simply price leaving the dome's edge. It is also wrongly assumed to take as long as a rounding bottom; tops typically form faster.
concept.example: After a multi-year uptrend, a stock's monthly closes arc over a dome between $80 and $95 for a year, volume swelling at both ends; when price slides off the right edge of the dome below $80, the distribution pattern is considered confirmed.

citations.source: The Economic Times, ET Wealth: Why rounding bottoms & tops formations are more predictable and reliable than V-shaped formations
